newsitem.title: BELGIUM: EU agrees to label gene farm products from July 31.
newsitem.headline: EU agrees to label gene farm products from July 31.

text.p: The European Commission on Wednesday formally approved the compulsory labelling of all genetically-modified farm products from July 31, 1997.
A Commission official said only one EU member state opposed the move, arguing that the deadline for implementation was too short.
The new labelling rules, proposed by the Commission on April 2, require labels specifying the product "may contain or may consist of genetically modified organisms." (GMOs)
Products containing a mixture of GMOs and conventional organisms will also have to be labelled.
In a statement, EU Environment Commissioner Ritt Bjerregaard described GMO labelling as "a valuable information for the consumer and not as a warning."
Bjerregaard thanked biotech companies which had co-operated and agreed to label their GMO products even though they were not obliged to do so as the new rules are not retroactive.

"The recent approval of two (rapeseed) products from PGS Plant Genetic Systems underlines that labelling clearly makes a strong difference in the somewhat cumbersome and delicate process of approving GMOs," she said.
The Commission said that Agrevo, which has applied for rapeseed and maize, and Monsanto, for maize, seemed to have met the new labelling requirements.
It added that two other companies, Pioneer and Novartis which have applied for maize, had also to a certain extent responded positively.
Bjerregaard asked them to consider labelling bulk mixed consignments of GMO and non-GMO products as well as seed bags.
Valio Oy has said it will label a milk test kit and Dutch firm Bejo Zaden BV offered in January to label its gene-altered chicory.
The Commission is due to propose a comprehensive revision of an EU Directive on the release of GMOs into the environment before the summer break in August.
